answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts. Example ARM/Bicep type string: "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts" (e.g. resource id: /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/<accountName>).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: CLI group: az cosmosdb. Commands: az cosmosdb create, az cosmosdb show, az cosmosdb keys list, az cosmosdb update, az cosmosdb database create. This is in the core Azure CLI (no separate extension required for basic account management). Example: az cosmosdb create -g myRg -n myAccount --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts" (example declaration: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName ... }). Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "acct" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible Cosmos connection string (standard): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. SRV-style: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Port: 10255 for direct TLS connections. Required options commonly: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false. Use the account's username/password from the portal or keys as the Mongo username/password.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB billing model: Request Units (RU/s) are the canonical billing unit for provisioned throughput; you can provision fixed RU/s per database/collection or use autoscale. There is also a serverless option (pay per RU consumed) for some account/configurations. For MongoDB compatibility you typically provision RU/s (or autoscale RU) at container or database level. (Note: some newer SKUs offer vCore-like compute tiers for 'managed MongoDB' offerings, but the standard Cosmos model is RU-based.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary supported data-plane auth for the MongoDB API: username/password (SCRAM) using credentials managed by the Cosmos account (usernames derived from account keys or created Mongo users). Management-plane operations (creating accounts, RBAC) use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID). Native Azure AD (Entra) authentication for the MongoDB wire protocol is not generally available for standard MongoDB drivers; you authenticate the driver with the Mongo credentials in the connection string. To use Azure AD identities for management/API calls, obtain an AAD token with az login or azure.identity and call the management REST/az cli APIs. (If you need AAD-backed DB auth, you'd typically use a Cosmos SQL API or a custom proxy.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API use the standard MongoDB drivers. Example for Python: use pymongo (pip install pymongo). For .NET use the official MongoDB.Driver NuGet. There are Azure SDKs for Cosmos DB (azure-cosmos) but if you target the MongoDB API you should use the MongoDB driver to talk to the account endpoint.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: I believe vector index support (if present) exposes HNSW, IVF and disk-ANN variants. A MongoDB-style createIndex would look similar to: db.fraud_vectors.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'ivf', metric: 'cosine', dims: 1536, name: 'embedding_ivf' }). Concretely: db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', m:16, efConstruction:200, metric:'l2' }). NOTE: exact option names vary by vendor; expect options like algorithm, metric, dims/size, and tuning params (m, efConstruction, numLists).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Options: 1) Use MongoDB text indexes for simple full-text queries (db.collection.createIndex({ field:'text' }) and $text queries). 2) For richer semantic/hybrid search on Azure, use Azure Cognitive Search and index documents in the Cosmos DB account (or push data into Search) to combine vector/semantic retrieval. If the managed Mongo-compatible service exposes vector indexes, you combine a vector search with text/metadata filters in your application layer to produce hybrid results. There is no single out-of-the-box "hybrid" operator in the MongoDB API; you typically run a vector search then re-rank with textual similarity or call Azure Cognitive Search for semantic ranking.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports specific MongoDB server versions (for example historically 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, later 5.0; newer accounts may support 6.x). Not all MongoDB features are implemented—common omissions historically include server-side JavaScript (db.eval), some admin commands, certain aggregation operators, multi-document transactions across partitions (limited or with constraints), and filesystem-level features. Expect subtle differences in aggregation pipeline behavior and some commands, so test your workload. (Pick the API version when creating the account; drivers must be compatible with the account's supported wire version.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for the SQL API but it historically does NOT support the MongoDB API. For MongoDB-compatible development, use the official MongoDB server Docker image locally (e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:6.0) and connect on port 27017. Use a local mongo instance for fast iteration and then test against the real Azure cluster for compatibility.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Support for change streams is limited historically. Some versions of the Cosmos MongoDB API exposed a change-feed/CDC capability, but MongoDB-style changeStreams were not always fully supported. If supported for your account/API version you may need to enable the feature or use the account-level Change Feed / CDC integration. Expect to verify support for your chosen server-version when creating the account; do not assume changeStreams are available without checking. (If change streams are unavailable, use the Cosmos Change Feed or Azure Functions connectors.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: I expect there is a service-specific MCP server named something like "documentdb" (or 'cosmosdb') for data-plane inspection and agent tools. The general Azure MCP server handles resource management (ARM) but a dedicated documentdb/cosmosdb MCP server is required to offer Mongo-level data-plane tooling (collection/index listing, explain plans). So use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations; general Azure MCP covers only management-plane.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically "DocumentDB" was the original name for the database service that eventually became Azure Cosmos DB (SQL API). Azure Cosmos DB is the umbrella service that supports multiple APIs (SQL/DocumentDB, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). The Microsoft "DocumentDB" name refers to the older SQL API engine and is distinct from any open-source project called DocumentDB; the Microsoft service is a proprietary engine that exposes multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft's proprietary Cosmos DB engine with a MongoDB protocol compatibility layer (i.e., not a stock MongoDB server). For most driver-based apps using supported features the changes are minimal: use standard MongoDB drivers and connection strings. However, differences exist in features, aggregation semantics, transactions, and limits; test critical pipelines and avoid relying on unimplemented commands. Also performance and consistency are governed by Cosmos settings (consistency levels, RU consumption).

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a collection named "fraud_vectors" in database "sample_fintech_01" and add a vector index on field "embedding". Example mongo-shell-like command I would run: db.getSiblingDB('sample_fintech_01').fraud_vectors.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_ivf', algorithm: 'ivf', metric: 'cosine', dims: 1536, numLists: 1024 }). (Adjust dims and tuning params to match embedding dimension; many providers accept algorithm/metric/numLists options.)

answers.question: Which Python client and connection code will the sample use to connect at runtime?
answers.answer:
Use pymongo. Connection code I would use: from pymongo import MongoClient
import os
uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']
# ensure the URI contains tls/ssl and retryWrites flags
client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=False)
db = client['sample_fintech_01']
# collection: db.fraud_vectors

answers.question: How will the sample perform a vector search from Python?
answers.answer:
I will call a server-side vector-search command exposed by the Mongo endpoint. Example pattern (pseudo-command):
query = { 'vectorSearch': 'fraud_vectors', 'vector': query_vector, 'k': 10, 'field': 'embedding', 'metric': 'cosine', 'algorithm': 'ivf' }
result = db.command(query)
If the service exposes a collection-level helper, I'd use db.fraud_vectors.runCommand('vectorSearch', {...}) or a driver-level API if provided. Then map returned ids/scores into documents for explanation.

answers.question: How will embeddings be stored in documents for this sample?
answers.answer: Store embeddings as a dense array of floats in the field "embedding" (e.g. "embedding": [0.0012, -0.543, ...]). Normalize embeddings to unit length if using cosine similarity. Example document schema: { _id: ObjectId(...), transaction_id: 'tx123', features: {...}, embedding: [float,...], label: 'fraud'|'benign', metadata: {...} }

answers.question: How will authentication for the sample be handled in code and CI?
answers.answer: The app will read the full MongoDB connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient. Do not hard-code keys; for CI use secret storage (Azure Key Vault or CI secret variables) to populate DOCUMENTDB_URI. Example: export DOCUMENTDB_URI='mongodb://<user>:<pw>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false' then in Python: client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']).
